headline: Slowing growth
body: It sounds like a contradiction and it's the most useful idea in this topic.
punch: And researchers deliberately tested whether it generalises.

headline: The original finding
body: Hypothyroidism slows chondrocyte proliferation in rats — and it also slows growth plate senescence. The plate ages more slowly while it grows more slowly.
punch: Which could have been a thyroid-specific quirk.

headline: So they tested
body: The follow-up asked whether delayed senescence is a general consequence of growth inhibition from any cause, rather than something particular to thyroid hormone.
punch: The right question to ask of a surprising result.

headline: It generalises
body: Growth inhibition from unrelated mechanisms delays senescence the same way. What matters is that proliferation slowed — not what slowed it.
punch: The cause is irrelevant. The rate is everything.

headline: Which confirms
body: Senescence tracks cumulative proliferation history, not calendar age. That's the assumption underneath treating growth plate exhaustion as the mechanism of fusion.
punch: Your plates count divisions, not birthdays.

headline: And it explains
body: Suppress growth temporarily and the plate spends its reserve slower. Release the suppression and growth rate exceeds normal for age, because more capacity remains.

headline: But note the asymmetry
body: Slowed proliferation is recoverable. Structural depletion of the progenitor pool — as estrogen causes — is not. Two suppressions can look identical and end differently.
punch: A growth chart cannot tell you which one happened.

headline: Which is why
body: Anything accelerating growth velocity also accelerates the spending of a finite reserve. The interventions that preserve height are frequently the ones that slow things down.
punch: The counter-intuitive answer is the correct one here.
